title: Netflix Takes On Media Giants As Video Streaming War Goes Global | Stock News & Stock Market Analysis - IBD
text:

And, Iger explains how the pending deal to acquire film and other assets from 21st Century Fox Entertainment ( FOXA ) will give Disney more heft to fight Netflix and others. 
"The films that our studio makes in 2019 and beyond will be sublicensed or licensed to our own platform," Iger explained. "It's ultimately our intention, and this (Fox) acquisition clearly will enable this even more, to create and to ultimately grow a global direct-to-consumer business that will take advantage of the production output that the combined companies will have." 
The big, diversified media giants no longer take Netflix lightly. Instead, they're revving up for video streaming wars worldwide. 
Advantage Netflix. It already operates a global, direct-to-consumer platform while Disney aspires to have one. Streaming Over There 
Netflix stock has jumped 70% in 2018, propelling IBD's Leisure-Movies & Related group to No. 3 on Thursday among the 197 industry groups tracked by IBD . The Media-Diversified group — which includes Disney, Time Warner and 21st Century Fox — ranked No. 122. 
Netflix plans to spend up to $8 billion in 2018 on programming, including 700 original TV shows and movies. It has increased investment in local content, such as the thriller "Dark" from Germany and "Club de Cuervos" from Mexico. In 2018, Netflix plans to have 30 local language originals, up from 8 last year. 
When Netflix reported fourth-quarter earnings on Jan. 22 , international growth "was the highlight of the print," said Ralph Schackart, an analyst at William Blair. "Since Netflix's expansion into 130 additional countries two years ago, its international streaming businesses appear to be inflecting." 
Netflix expanded into Latin America in 2011 and Europe in 2012, but 2016 marked its big move. In January of that year, Netflix expanded into little Albania and a host of other countries. 
In Q4, Netflix added 4.9 million international subscribers vs. 1.45 million in the U.S. Netflix added 18.5 million international subscribers cross all of 2017, accelerating from 14.3 million in 2016 and 11.7 million in 2015. 
That's vital, because Netflix garners revenue only from subscription fees, not advertising. 
Netflix ended 2017 with 117.5 million subscribers, with 62 million of them outside the U.S. 
"I think all of the media companies need to look at what Netflix is doing globally, because it's going to change the content economics, Michael White, the former CEO of Satellite TV broadcaster DirecTV told CNBC in a Feb. 28 interview. "If Netflix gets 200 million subscribers from international, they'll be writing much bigger checks (for content) in Hollywood." 
Netflix's reach is growing with pay-TV partners. U.K.-based satellite TV broadcaster Sky on March 1 said it will integrate a Netflix app into its set-top boxes. Sky has 23 million subscribers in Europe. U.S.-based Comcast ( CMCSA ) and Fox are now in a bidding war for a controlling stake in Sky. 
And, some big targets are still up there for grabs. Netflix has steered away from China. But, in 2017 it reached a licensing deal for its original programming with iQiyi, the video streaming business of Baidu ( BIDU ), the Chinese internet search giant. Baidu's iQiyi in February filed for an initial public offering in the U.S. 
Then, there's India. Netflix has roughly half a million subscribers in India, estimates IHS Markit. 
Netflix CEO Reed Hastings, speaking at a media panel in New Delhi in February, said: "Given the consumer base, the next 100 million (subscribers) for us is coming from India." 
In India, Netflix faces competition from local video streaming services as well as a strong U.S. rival — Amazon Prime Video. Amazon.com's streaming service, in fact, is also a strong rival to Netflix in Germany, Japan and the U.K., says IHS Markit. 
Amazon had 30 million U.S. video subscribers in 2017, estimates IHS. Amazon Prime Video operates in 16 countries and has 11 million subscribers from Germany, Japan and the U.K., it says. In those three countries, Amazon has more subscribers than Netflix, says IHS. 
Amazon in February licensed content from Disney India, including Marvel movies. For Japan, also in February, Amazon licensed content from Time Warner's HBO. The same month Amazon inked an original production deal for Latin America with Televisa. 
Max Signorelli, an analyst at IHS, told IBD that Amazon's strategy of acquiring "live sports content may start to set itself apart from the on-demand libraries of Netflix." 
Bulls, though, say that Netflix's high-quality content library will enable it to compete with traditional TV networks around the world. Netflix's international growth may not peak until 2020 or 2021, analysts say. Brand Strength Vs. Creative Talent 
Meanwhile, big media firms will continue shifting their content to platforms like Hulu — a joint venture of Fox, Disney, Comcast and Time Warner — as well as their own stand-alone internet services. Netflix, facing the challenge to fuel U.S. and international subscriber growth, is pushing for more big hits in original programming. 
Amazon, for its part, failed to win a single Emmy award in September as Netflix and Hulu walked away with a combined multitude of wins. (HBO still ruled, taking home 29 Emmys, vs. 20 for Netflix.) 
Disney's Iger says its main advantage is already having box-office powerhouses such as Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars. That gives the company strong brands to leverage when it launches direct-to-consumer streaming services, Iger says. 
But Netflix's content team has a proven knack for picking hits, names such as "Stranger Things" and "House of Cards", when bidding for first-run TV shows. And, Netflix is sticking with its pioneering strategy of releasing a full season of TV shows all at once, luring the rising 'binge-watching' audience. 
Netflix aims to hire away the best in the business as it competes for high-quality content. 
Netflix in February poached Ryan Murphy, creator of "American Horror Story" and other hits, from Fox in a five-year, $300 million deal. Netflix earlier inked a multiyear deal with showrunner Shonda Rhimes, the mastermind behind "Grey's Anatomy," "Scandal" and other TV shows at Disney's ABC. 
In 2019, Netflix plans to debut its most ambitious film to date: Martin Scorsese's gangster movie "The Irishman." "Look for 'The Irishman' to be the movie industry's disruption equivalent of what Netflix's 'House of Cards' did to the television industry in 2013," said BTIG Research in a report. 
Netflix depends on the high-yield bond market to fund its huge and growing content investments. The company has some $6.5 billion in long-term debt with content liabilities at another $3.4 billion. 
In October, Netflix sold $1.6 billion in bonds, its largest deal ever. That pushed its debt-to-equity ratio above 180%. The number is well above Disney or 21 st Century Fox, but in line with television competitors such as Discovery Communications ( DICSA ) and AMC Networks ( AMCX ). 
The video streaming titan is expected to have free cash flow burn in a range of $3 billion to $4 billion in 2018 vs. $2 billion last year. Disney has told analysts its negative FCF will persist for several years. If so, rising interest rates could become a problem. In a sign of increasing competition, Netflix plans to spend $2 billion in marketing in 2018, up almost 54%. A Failure To Go Hostile 
With its reliance on subscription fees, Netflix' pricing power has always been an issue. 
Netflix in October hiked prices for subscribers in the U.S., the U.K., France and Germany. December quarter subscriber growth in those countries was impressive just the same, analysts say. In Asia, though, stiff competition has kept Netflix more cautious about hiking prices. 
Netflix's stock plunged in 2011 when it made one of its few missteps – hiking monthly subscriber fees before it provided perks such as original programming. 
Cable TV pioneer John Malone, as well as others, that year missed what was maybe their best chance to buy Netflix. Malone's business empire now spans Liberty Media, Liberty Global ( LBTYA ), Charter Communications ( CHTR ), Discovery Communications, and Lions Gate Entertainment ( LGFA ). 
Asked in 2015 at an investor conference what his biggest mistake ever was, Malone answered: "I would say the biggest one in the last few years was not going hostile on Netflix when we identified it as undervalued." 
Media consolidation is now rife, with Disney agreeing to buy assets from Fox, and AT&T ( T ) aiming to buy Time Warner, if the telecom conglomerate can beat the Department of Justice in federal court. 
Citigroup in December said there's a 40% chance that Apple ( AAPL ) will acquire Netflix. The internet TV provider's market valuation has shot above $127 billion, with this year's gain. That's a lot of money even for Apple.
